Unit 1 — The Elements of Art — Teacher Cycle Plan

Teacher-facing. Benchmark codes and answer keys live here only — never on student pages.

Course: 2-D Studio Art · CPALMS 0101300 · Grades 9–12 · Full-year, async Canvas

Cycle: Q1 · Unit 1 of 16 · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week

Featured work: Vincent van Gogh, The Bedroom, 1889, Art Institute of Chicago (public domain)

Studio project / ladder rung: Design Your Dream Room — variation rung

REVISION NOTES (this pass, 2026-07-15)

This unit was revised from the 03_Development draft per the subject-matter reviewer's notes. Changes made:

1. Value element image gap closed. The reviewer flagged that "value" appeared in Part 2 with no image connecting it to its definition. Added a verified real photograph — NASA Artemis II crew, Shadows Across Vavilov Crater (lunar surface, April 6, 2026), public domain U.S. government work, sourced via Wikimedia Commons — directly under the "Value: the workhorse element" section, with a paragraph tying the photo's light/shadow gradient back to the value-scale concept. The featured Van Gogh work and the original SVG/CSS Elements-of-Art diagrams (Line, Shape, Form, Space, Color, Texture) were already original hand-built diagrams, not AI-generated, and were left as-is.

2. VR Session redesigned. Replaced the old "load a pre-made snapshot" pattern. Students now choose ONE real, verified artwork from a short list (or bring their own free choice, teacher-approved), look it up online, and pull the image into their own VR space themselves before running DAIJ on it. This is more authentic critique practice and matches the redesign applied across the course. VR example options (all public domain, all verified against the holding museum's own collection page):

- Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night, 1889, Museum of Modern Art — https://www.moma.org/collection/works/79802

- Katsushika Hokusai, Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave), c. 1830–32, Metropolitan Museum of Art — https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/45434

- Johannes Vermeer, Girl with a Pearl Earring, c. 1665, Mauritshuis — https://www.mauritshuis.nl/en/our-collection/artworks/670-girl-with-a-pearl-earring

- Rembrandt van Rijn, Self-Portrait as the Apostle Paul, 1661, Rijksmuseum — https://www.rijksmuseum.nl/en/collection/object/Self-portrait-as-the-Apostle-Paul--4faa97ed774e6e3f81b76cf3aed6226d

3. Gallery Manners added. Because this is the course's first-ever VR encounter, a Gallery Manners line was added to "Before you enter" (stand back, don't touch, gallery-level voice, leave room for others). This note is intentionally NOT repeated in later units — it is taught once, here, and carries forward.

4. No change to the group-work / "if you are in a live session, share with a classmate" line (explicitly out of scope this pass).

NGSSS benchmarks addressed (from course map, Q1 set)

  • VA.912.O.1.1 — Use the structural elements of art and organizational principles in the creation of works.
  • VA.912.C.1.1 — Use art-criticism vocabulary to describe and analyze visual works (DAIJ).
  • VA.912.S.3.4 / S.1.3 — Use accurate art vocabulary and develop skills/techniques during studio work.
  • VA.912.H.1.1 — Analyze how artworks reflect their culture, time, and place (Van Gogh, Arles, 1889).

Remaining Q1 map standards (C.1.3, C.2.1, H.2.2, O.2.1, S.2.1) are carried across Units 2–4. See course-shared standards tracker.

Pacing against the 250 min/week budget

Week 1 (Learn & Look ≈ 250 min): lesson page reading + visuals (~55 min) · Sketch: Value Scale + Element Hunt (~40 min) · VR Element Gallery Critique (~30 min) · Quiz + review (~20 min) · independent studio brainstorming/practice (~100 min).

Week 2 (Make & Reflect ≈ 250 min): Design Your Dream Room studio work + artist statement (the graded assessment). Self-paced across the week.

Teacher grading load

ONE teacher-graded pass this cycle: the Dream Room artwork + artist statement on the 5-row rubric (~5 min/student). Sketch, VR, and quiz are completion- or auto-scored.

Quiz answer key

1-B · 2-B · 3-C · 4-B · 5-C · 6-True · 7 (Line→path of a moving point; Form→illusion of a 3-D object; Color→light as hue/value/intensity; Space→area within/around/between objects) · 8-B.

Copyright check (per OAO Copyright Policy 2026)

  • The Bedroom (Van Gogh, d. 1890) is public domain — may be displayed in full with attribution + source link. Verified against the Art Institute of Chicago's own public API (artic.edu/artworks/28560; `is_public_domain: true`; image_id `6644829f-f292-c5c4-a73c-0356a6fdbf0d` matches the embedded IIIF URL).
  • Shadows Across Vavilov Crater (NASA, 2026) is a U.S. government work, public domain, verified via its Wikimedia Commons file page.
  • The four VR example artworks (Van Gogh, Hokusai, Vermeer, Rembrandt) are all by artists deceased well over 70 years — public domain. Each museum collection-page URL above was verified live before inclusion.
  • All inline Elements-of-Art diagrams (Line, Shape, Form, Space, Color, Texture cards) are original HTML/CSS/SVG built with design tokens — no third-party images, no AI-generated images.
  • No in-copyright artists appear in Unit 1.

Unit 2 — Prehistoric Cave Art & the Power of Line — Teacher Cycle Plan

Teacher-facing. Benchmark codes and answer keys live here only — never on student pages.

Course: 2-D Studio Art · CPALMS 0101300 · Grades 9–12 · Full-year, async Canvas

Cycle: Q1 · Unit 2 of 16 · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week

Featured work (embedded on student page): polychrome bison, Altamira cave ceiling, Cantabria, Spain, c. 36,000–15,000 BCE (public domain; attributed to the Magdalenian culture, not an individual). Secondary reference (teacher plan / VR only): Hall of the Bulls, Lascaux cave, Montignac, Dordogne, France, c. 17,000 BCE.

Studio project / ladder rung: Contour Animal Drawing — study/copy of the cave painters' confident contour, then variation onto a student-chosen animal.

Element focus: Line (contour, blind contour, continuous, gesture, line weight/quality, cross-contour).

REVISION NOTES (this pass, 2026-07-15)

This unit was revised from the 03_Development draft per the subject-matter reviewer's notes. Changes made:

1. Part 2 line-concept imagery upgraded for realism. The reviewer asked for a "more realistic feel" in Part 2. The Contour Line card and the Gesture Line card were swapped from abstract SVG diagrams to real, verified public-domain photographs that directly demonstrate the concept:

- Contour Line now shows a real photograph of a young American bison in profile (a single clean edge, tying back to the Altamira bison theme). Photographer Ryan Hagerty, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; released into the public domain by the author, verified on its Wikimedia Commons file page.

- Gesture Line now shows Eadweard Muybridge's The Horse in Motion (1878), the historic stop-motion photograph sequence of a galloping horse. Public domain (published before 1931; Library of Congress holding), verified on its Wikimedia Commons file page.

- Continuous Line, Line Weight/Quality, Cross-Contour, and Line Direction were left as their original hand-built SVG diagrams. These are original, geometrically deliberate diagrams (not AI-generated), which satisfies the course's Part 2 imagery policy on its own; they were not the cards the reviewer's "more realistic" note was aimed at.

2. VR Session redesigned. Replaced the old "load a pre-made snapshot" pattern. Students now choose ONE real, verified cave-art (or other ancient/cultural) work from a short list, or bring their own free choice with teacher approval, look it up online, and pull the image into their own VR space themselves before running DAIJ. VR example options (all public domain, anonymous/cultural authorship, facts verified against current sources):

- Bison, Cave of Altamira, Cantabria, Spain (same work featured on the lesson page)

- Hall of the Bulls, Lascaux Cave, Dordogne, France (c. 17,000–20,000 years old; official site: https://archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/lascaux/en/lascaux-cave-virtual-visit)

- Lion Panel, Chauvet Cave, Ardeche, France (c. 30,000–36,500 years old; official site: https://archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/chauvet/en/large-lion-panel)

- Spotted Horses Panel, Pech Merle Cave, Lot, France (c. 24,640 years old; site: https://en.pechmerle.com/the-prehistory-center/the-pech-merle-cave/)

- This unit does NOT repeat the Gallery Manners line (taught once, in Unit 1 only, per course convention).

3. No change to the group-work / "if you are in a live session, compare with a classmate" line (explicitly out of scope this pass). No change to the featured Altamira bison embed, which was already correctly sourced and verified.

NGSSS benchmarks addressed (from course map, Q1 set)

  • VA.912.H.1.1 — Analyze how artworks reflect the culture, time, and place of their making (prehistoric cave painting; cave art credited to culture/period, not named individuals).
  • VA.912.S.1.3 — Use accurate art-making skills and processes during studio work (contour and line-weight technique).
  • VA.912.S.3.4 — Use accurate art vocabulary and develop technical skill through studio practice (contour animal drawing).
  • VA.912.C.1.1 — Use art-criticism vocabulary to describe and analyze visual works (DAIJ on the Hall of the Bulls; line vocabulary).
  • VA.912.O.1.1 — Use the structural element of line and organizational choices in the creation of a work.

Q1 map standards carried/distributed across Units 1–4: C.1.3, C.2.1, H.2.2, O.2.1, S.2.1. Unit 1 anchored O.1.1/C.1.1/S.3.4/S.1.3/H.1.1; Unit 2 deepens line-specific S and H. See course-shared standards tracker.

Pacing against the 250 min/week budget

Week 1 (Learn & Look ≈ 250 min): lesson page reading + visuals (~55 min) · Sketch: Blind Contour + Continuous Line (~30 min) · VR Cave-Art Gallery Critique + contour animal (~30 min) · Quiz + review (~20 min) · independent contour-line practice and gesture warm-ups / studio brainstorming (~115 min).

Week 2 (Make & Reflect ≈ 250 min): Contour Animal Drawing studio work + artist statement (the graded assessment). Gesture warm-ups, photo selection, then the finished varied-contour drawing. Self-paced across the week.

Teacher grading load

ONE teacher-graded pass this cycle: the Contour Animal Drawing + artist statement on the 5-row rubric (~5 min/student). Sketch, VR, and quiz are completion- or auto-scored.

Quiz answer key

1-B (Lascaux) · 2-C (~17,000 years) · 3-B (Altamira) · 4-B (charcoal and ochre) · 5-C (contour line) · 6-True · 7 (Blind contour→looking only at the object, not the paper; Continuous line→one unbroken line; Gesture line→fast loose marks capturing motion; Ochre→natural earth pigment) · 8-C (contour line with varied line weight).

Copyright check (per OAO Copyright Policy 2026)

  • Embedded image (lesson page): the polychrome bison from the Altamira cave ceiling (Cantabria, Spain; Upper Paleolithic, c. 36,000–15,000 BCE). Embedded via `` from Wikimedia Commons using the stable redirect `https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Altamira,%20bison.jpg` (Commons file: `File:Altamira, bison.jpg`). Re-verified this pass against the file's Wikimedia Commons page: public domain, ancient cultural work. Credited to the Magdalenian culture, not an individual.
  • New Part 2 photographs (re-verified this pass): American bison photograph (Ryan Hagerty, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, released to public domain by the author) and Eadweard Muybridge's The Horse in Motion high-resolution scan (public domain, pre-1931 publication, Library of Congress source via Wikimedia Commons). Both confirmed on their respective Wikimedia Commons file pages before use.
  • Lascaux Hall of the Bulls, Chauvet Lion Panel, and Pech Merle Spotted Horses are referenced only as VR example options (students look them up themselves) and in the teacher plan; none are embedded on the student lesson page. All three are ancient/anonymous cultural works, safely public domain, with official site URLs verified live this pass (see Revision Notes above).
  • Facts verified against current sources cross-referenced across the French Ministry of Culture's official cave sites, the Pech Merle prehistory center's official site, and standard art-history references: Altamira near Santillana del Mar, Cantabria, Spain, polychrome bison ceiling, c. 36,000–15,000 years old; Lascaux near Montignac, Dordogne, France, c. 17,000–20,000 years old, black auroch bulls dominant; Chauvet, Ardeche, France, c. 30,000–36,500 years old, lion-hunting panel; Pech Merle, Lot, France, spotted horses panel c. 24,640 years old.

Unit 3 — Islamic Art: Pattern, Balance & Symmetry — Teacher Cycle Plan

Teacher-facing. Benchmark codes and answer keys live here only — never on student pages.

Course: 2-D Studio Art · CPALMS 0101300 · Grades 9–12 · Full-year, async Canvas

Cycle: Q1 · Unit 3 of 16 · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week

Featured work (embedded): Tile with 'Saz' Leaf Design, Ottoman period, Iznik, Turkey, ca. 1545 to 55, stonepaste glazed ceramic — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Richard Ettinghausen, 1978, Public Domain (CC0); attributed to culture/period, not an individual. Tilework of the Alhambra (Nasrid Granada, 14th c.) and the Dome of the Rock (Jerusalem, late 7th c.) are referenced in text as comparable examples and are appropriate for the VR gallery.

Studio project / ladder rung: Islamic Tile Design — study/copy a motif, then variation rung.

Revision notes (04_Final pass — what changed and why)

This unit was revised from the 03_Development draft per the reviewer audit and the shared revision brief. Two changes were made; nothing else in the unit needed correction.

1. Reviewer's "the Start" note, resolved. The reviewer flag reading "the Start" is confirmed a typo for "the Star" — the star-pattern construction exercise already named in the lesson's Section 2 heading, "The hidden grid: where the stars come from" (the circle → guide-line → star sequence). On inspection, that sequence was already built as original inline SVG diagrams, not AI-generated raster images, so it already satisfies the course's non-AI-feel imagery policy. No replacement of those diagrams was needed.

2. Added one real, verified photograph to Part 2 directly after the star-construction sequence, so the schematic steps are immediately followed by evidence that this is how real historic walls were actually built. Image: geometric and arabesque wall ornament, Nasrid period (14th century), Patio de los Arrayanes (Court of the Myrtles), the Alhambra, Granada, Spain. Photograph by Jebulon (Wikimedia Commons), 2010, released by the photographer into the public domain. Verified directly against the file's Wikimedia Commons page before use. This directly answers the reviewer's ask for "real, relatable imagery, not AI-generated" in Part 2.

3. VR Session redesigned per the course-wide VR revision (see below). The old "load a pre-made snapshot" pattern is replaced with: the student chooses one of four real, verified Islamic geometric works (or a teacher-approved work of their own), sources an image of it themselves, and pulls it into their own VR space to run the DAIJ critique. Everything else about the VR Session (Before You Enter / Look / Respond / Make structure, completion grading, solo-async-first) is unchanged.

4. Sketch, Quiz, and Studio Project were already compliant and are unchanged from the 03_Development draft.

NGSSS benchmarks addressed (from course map, Q1 set)

  • VA.912.H.1.1 — Analyze how artworks reflect their culture, time, and place (Islamic geometric ornament; Alhambra, Nasrid Granada, 14th c.).
  • VA.912.O.1.1 — Use the structural elements of art and organizational principles (pattern, balance, symmetry) in the creation of works.
  • VA.912.C.2.1 — Use art-criticism strategies to reflect on and evaluate works (DAIJ on a tile panel).
  • VA.912.S.2.1 — Develop and refine skills/techniques in studio work (compass-and-straightedge grid construction).

Element focus: Shape (geometric vs organic, positive shape / negative space, figure-ground, silhouette, abstracted shape)

Studio project / ladder rung: Personal Identity Collage — variation rung

REVISION NOTE (this pass)

The prior 03_Development draft featured The Snail (1953, Tate, London). Per the reviewer's note and the revision brief, the featured work was swapped to Memory of Oceania (MoMA). All surrounding text was rewritten to match the new work: the Look First description, the Wonder callout, the reflect widget's four response options, the Name What You See section (geometric/organic mix, positive/negative space, silhouette/abstracted shape paragraphs), the full DAIJ walkthrough (Describe/Analyze/Interpret/Judge), the Try It widget's feedback text, the VR Session's example-artwork list, the Quiz Q6 stem, and the studio project's opening line. No stale references to snail shapes, spirals, or the Tate remain — verified by a full re-read of `lesson.html` and `canvas-items.md` after the rewrite.

Date correction: the pre-revision brief for this unit listed 1946 as the work's date. MoMA's own collection record (verified live, see below) dates it "Nice-Cimiez, Hôtel Régina, summer 1952-early 1953." This plan and the lesson page use the verified MoMA date, not 1946.

Why this work instead of The Snail: Memory of Oceania is arguably a stronger fit for the Personal Identity Collage project than The Snail was. It is literally Matisse encoding a specific personal memory (his 1930 trip to Tahiti, recalled more than twenty years later) into a sparse arrangement of abstracted shapes and a great deal of negative space — the same move students are asked to make about their own lives and identities in the Week 2 project. It also lets the lesson teach positive/negative space more vividly, since roughly nine-tenths of the composition is open ground.

REVISION NOTE (this pass)

The reviewer flagged the Starry Night image as not displaying. Root cause identified: the prior `` pointed at the Wikimedia `Special:FilePath` redirect for the full-resolution master scan, which is a genuine file but resolves to an approximately 664 MB, 44,567 x 35,291 pixel JPEG — far too large to load reliably in a browser or an embedded Canvas iframe, and likely to time out or fail silently. The URL itself was not fake; it was simply pointing at the wrong (full-resolution) file.

Fix: the `` now points at Wikimedia's standard 1280px-wide thumbnail derivative of the same file (`.../thumb/e/ea/Van_Gogh_-_Starry_Night_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/1280px-Van_Gogh_-_Starry_Night_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg`). This was fetched and visually confirmed at build time to render correctly as a clean, full-color reproduction of the painting. The Wikimedia Commons file page itself was also independently verified as a live, active page describing this exact file as a public-domain Google Art Project scan of the MoMA painting.

The figcaption also now cites MoMA's own collection record directly (verified live at build time: https://www.moma.org/collection/works/79802, "Vincent van Gogh. The Starry Night. Saint Rémy, June 1889 | MoMA"), confirming the holding institution, correct title, and date, in addition to the Wikimedia image source.

Also applied per the revision brief: the VR Session was redesigned from a "load a pre-made snapshot" pattern to a pull-your-own-artwork pattern (see below), and the Week 2 Studio Project's student-facing steps were expanded from 6 to 9, adding scaffolding without cutting any original content (see below).

assignments.title: Week 1 Sketch: Value Scale + Element Hunt
assignments.html:
This sketch is your practice rung, not a finished artwork. Artists train their eyes before their hands. Focus on effort and observation, not perfection. Do both parts on one sheet of paper (~30 minutes total).

Part 1 — Value Scale. Draw a row of 5 boxes, each about 1 inch wide. Fill box 1 as lightly as you can and box 5 as dark as your pencil will go. Make boxes 2, 3, and 4 even steps in between. Label the row "Lightest" to "Darkest."

Part 2 — Element Hunt. Look around the room you are sitting in. Find and quickly sketch:

  • one strong line (a window frame, a cord, an edge)
  • one geometric shape and one organic shape
  • one object where you can see value turning it into a 3-D form (light side, shadow side)

Label each find with the element it shows.

Submit: Photograph your sheet in good light (no shadow across the paper). Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive art portfolio folder: 2DArt_U01_Sketch_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort):

  • Both parts present on the sheet
  • Value scale shows 5 distinct steps
  • Element hunt items are labeled
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: Week 1 VR Session: Element Gallery Critique
assignments.html:
Before you enter: Have your vocabulary list and the four DAIJ steps (Describe, Analyze, Interpret, Judge) ready.

This is your first time entering a gallery in VR this year, so review Gallery Manners before you start: stand back from displayed work, don't touch, keep your voice at a gallery level, and leave room for others to see. These habits carry forward into every gallery critique this year.

Choose ONE real artwork that shows the Elements of Art at work. Pick from the list below, or bring in a different real work of your own choice with teacher approval:

  • Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night, 1889, Museum of Modern Art
  • Katsushika Hokusai, Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave), c. 1830 to 1832, Metropolitan Museum of Art
  • Johannes Vermeer, Girl with a Pearl Earring, c. 1665, Mauritshuis
  • Rembrandt van Rijn, Self-Portrait as the Apostle Paul, 1661, Rijksmuseum

Look up your chosen artwork online so you have a clear image of it, then pull that image into your own VR space (use your VR app's image or photo import tool) and open any gallery Location you like to display it.

Part 1 — Look (about 10 min). Move close to your chosen artwork inside VR. Using your VR drawing/note tool, place short notes beside it answering:

  1. Describe: What is literally shown?
  2. Analyze: Which 2–3 elements (line, shape, form, space, value, color, texture) is the artist leaning on?
  3. Interpret: What feeling or idea does it give you?
  4. Judge: Does it work? Why?

Part 2 — Respond (about 8 min). Answer aloud (record a short voice note) or in writing: "If you could keep only THREE of the seven elements for the rest of your life as an artist, which would you keep, and what could you still make with them?" If you are in a live session, share with a classmate and respond to one other answer.

Part 3 — Make (about 7 min). Use the VR drawing tool to sketch a quick 5-step value scale in the air, lightest to darkest. This is the same scale you will paint with this year.

Submit: Take a screenshot inside VR showing your notes or your value scale, and upload it. (No screenshot tool? Write 2–3 sentences describing what you did, including which artwork you chose.) Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder.

Grading: Completion. Evidence of all three parts attempted.

assignments.title: Week 2 Studio Project: Design Your Dream Room
assignments.html:
You have read a master's room. Now build your own. Design and draw the interior of your dream room — real or imagined — using all seven Elements of Art on purpose.

Materials (home-accessible): drawing paper, pencil and eraser, and your choice of color media (colored pencils, markers, or paint). A digital drawing app with layers is an equally accepted option.

Elements focus: all 7, with deliberate attention to space (make the room feel deep), value (give your objects light and shadow), and shape.

Steps:

  1. Brainstorm your room. What is it for? What mood do you want a visitor to feel?
  2. Lightly draw the back wall, then the floor and side walls so the room has depth. Let edges lead the eye inward (you saw this in Van Gogh's floorboards).
  3. Add at least five objects that belong in your room. Use overlap and size so nearer things sit in front.
  4. Build value: pick one light source and shade each object's shadow side. Aim for a visible light-to-dark range.
  5. Add color and texture to set the mood.
  6. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • All 7 elements are present and used on purpose
  • The room reads as a believable space with depth
  • A clear light source creates value and form
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible
  • The work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2–3 sentences):

  • What is your room, and what mood did you want?
  • Name two elements you used on purpose and where.
  • What are you proud of, or what would you change?

Submit: Photograph or export your finished room as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: 2DArt_U01_DreamRoom_LastName.

assignments.title: Blind Contour + Continuous Line
assignments.html:
This sketch is your practice rung, not a finished artwork. Artists train their eyes before their hands. Focus on effort and honest looking, not perfection. Your drawings will look strange, and that is exactly right. Do both parts on one sheet of paper (~30 minutes total).

Part 1 — Blind Contour of a Shoe. Set one of your shoes in front of you. Put your pencil on the paper and fix your eyes on the shoe, not the page. Slowly trace its edge with your eyes while your pencil follows at the same speed. Do not lift your pencil and do not peek at your paper until you are done. Move slowly enough that your hand and eye stay together.

Part 2 — Continuous Line Drawing of Your Hand. Place your non-drawing hand flat or relaxed on the table. Draw it with one unbroken line, never lifting your pencil. You may glance at your paper this time, but keep the line continuous, looping back over itself wherever you need to.

Label Part 1 "Blind Contour" and Part 2 "Continuous Line."

Submit: Photograph your sheet in good light (no shadow across the paper). Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive art portfolio folder: 2DArt_U02_Sketch_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort, auto/completion-scored):

  • Both parts present on the sheet
  • The blind contour was clearly done without looking (it looks wild, not traced)
  • The hand was drawn with one continuous, unbroken line
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: Cave-Art Gallery Critique
assignments.html:
Before you enter: Have your vocabulary list and the four DAIJ steps (Describe, Analyze, Interpret, Judge) ready.

Choose ONE real prehistoric cave-art work that shows the power of line. Pick from the list below, or bring in a different real, ancient, or cultural work of your own choice with teacher approval:

  • Bison, cave ceiling, Cave of Altamira, Cantabria, Spain (the same work from this lesson, if you would like to look closer)
  • Hall of the Bulls, Lascaux Cave, Dordogne, France
  • Lion Panel, Chauvet Cave, Ardeche, France
  • Spotted Horses Panel, Pech Merle Cave, Lot, France

Look up your chosen work online so you have a clear image of it, then pull that image into your own VR space (use your VR app's image or photo import tool) and open any gallery Location you like to display it.

Part 1 — Look and run DAIJ (about 10 min). Move close to your chosen cave-art work inside VR. Using your VR drawing or note tool, place short notes beside it answering:

  1. Describe: What animal is shown, and what colors and marks do you see?
  2. Analyze: What kinds of line is the artist using (contour, gesture, varied line weight)? Where does the line get thick or thin?
  3. Interpret: What feeling or idea does the animal give you? Does it feel still or in motion?
  4. Judge: Does it work? Why?

Part 2 — Make (about 10 min). Use the VR drawing tool to draw your own cave animal using only contour line: one confident outline, no shading. Vary your line weight so the body feels heavy and the legs feel quick, the way the cave painters did. If you are in a live session, compare your line with a classmate's and say one thing you notice.

Part 3 — Reflect (about 5 min). Answer aloud (record a short voice note) or in writing: "Drawing in the air with no eraser is a lot like working on a cave wall. What did that limit force you to do differently?"

Submit: Take a screenshot inside VR showing your DAIJ notes or your contour animal, and upload it. (No screenshot tool? Write 2 to 3 sentences describing what you did, including which work you chose.) Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder.

Grading: Completion. Evidence of all three parts attempted.

assignments.title: Contour Animal Drawing + Artist Statement
assignments.html:
The cave painters had no eraser, no shading, and no color theory. They had a wall and a confident line, and it was enough to make animals that still feel alive thousands of years later. Now it is your turn. Draw a detailed contour drawing of an animal using varied line weight and no shading. Line does all the work.

Materials (home-accessible): drawing paper and a pencil (or pen). A digital drawing app with a pressure-sensitive or adjustable brush is an equally accepted option. You do not need any color or shading media for this project.

Line focus: contour line as the main structure, with deliberate line weight changes (thick where forms are heavy or close, thin where they are light or far) and cross-contour where it helps show roundness.

Steps:

  1. Choose your animal. Work from a photo or from life, not from memory, so your eye does the seeing.
  2. Warm up first with one quick gesture sketch to feel the animal's motion and proportion.
  3. Lightly place the big shapes, then commit to a clear contour line around the whole form and its main parts.
  4. Build line weight: press harder along heavy edges, shadowed sides, and where parts overlap; lighten your line on far or delicate edges.
  5. Add a few cross-contour lines if they help a rounded part read as solid. Do not shade.
  6. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • The animal is built from clear, confident contour line, not scribbled or traced timidly
  • Line weight varies on purpose and gives the drawing life and depth
  • No shading is used; line carries the whole image
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible
  • The work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • What animal did you draw, and why that one?
  • Name one place you varied your line weight on purpose and what it did.
  • What are you proud of, or what would you change?

Submit: Photograph or export your finished drawing as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: 2DArt_U02_ContourAnimal_LastName.

assignments.title: Grid + Radial Thumbnails
assignments.html:
This sketch is your practice rung, not a finished artwork. The geometry is the real skill here, so go slowly and let the tools do the work. Do both parts on one or two sheets of paper (~40 minutes total).

Part 1 — Construct the grid. Using a compass and a ruler, draw a circle about 4 inches across. Keep the compass set to the same width and step it around the edge of the circle to mark points. Connect points with your ruler to divide the circle into equal slices (aim for 8). This grid is the skeleton that every later line will follow. Do not erase your construction lines yet.

Part 2 — Develop 2 to 3 radial thumbnails. On top of (or beside) your grid, sketch 2 or 3 small, quick versions of a radial design. Study the 8-point star you saw in the lesson and copy its structure, then start a variation of your own: change which lines you trace, add a smaller star inside, or fill the spaces between with new shapes. Keep them rough. These are idea sketches for next week's tile.

Label your sheet with the rung: "Study and copy, then variation."

Submit: Photograph your sheet in good light (no shadow across the paper). Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive art portfolio folder: 2DArt_U03_Sketch_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort):

  • A compass-and-ruler grid is present, with visible construction lines
  • 2 to 3 radial thumbnails are drawn
  • At least one thumbnail shows a variation, not only a copy

assignments.title: Islamic Tile Design
assignments.html:
You have read a master surface and copied its structure. Now build your own. Design and draw a single square tile with a radial, symmetrical geometric pattern, then color it. Work the way the artisans did: let the geometry come first, then the color.

Materials (home-accessible): a compass, a ruler or straightedge, a sharp pencil and eraser, drawing paper, and your choice of color media (colored pencils, markers, or paint). A digital drawing app with a grid and shape tools is an equally accepted option.

Principles focus: pattern and balance above all, built on clean geometry, with deliberate symmetry. Use line and shape from your earlier units.

Steps:

  1. With your compass, draw a circle inside a square tile shape. Keep the compass set and step it around to mark equal points (try 8).
  2. Connect the points with your straightedge to build the grid. This is your skeleton.
  3. Trace selected lines to form a central motif, such as an 8-point star, so the design is the same as it turns around the center (radial balance).
  4. Repeat or extend shapes outward into the corners so the whole tile is filled and balanced. Check that the two halves mirror across the center (symmetry).
  5. Once the geometry is firm, color your tile. Use a small, planned set of colors and repeat them so the pattern reads clearly.
  6. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • A clear repeating motif built on real compass-and-ruler geometry
  • Radial balance: the design holds together around its center
  • Symmetry: the halves mirror cleanly
  • Color is planned and repeated, not random
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible
  • The work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • What is the motif at the center of your tile, and how did you build it?
  • Name where you used radial balance and symmetry on purpose.
  • What are you proud of, or what would you change?

Submit: Photograph or export your finished tile as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: 2DArt_U03_IslamicTile_LastName.

assignments.title: Value Scale + Shaded Sphere
assignments.html:
This sketch is your practice rung, not a finished artwork. Artists train their eyes before their hands. Focus on effort and observation, not perfection. Do both parts on one sheet of paper (~30 minutes total). Use pencil only, no color.

Part 1 — Value Scale. Draw a row of 5 boxes, each about 1 inch wide. Fill box 1 as lightly as you can and box 5 as dark as your pencil will go. Make boxes 2, 3, and 4 even steps in between. Label the row "Lightest" to "Darkest."

Part 2 — Shaded Sphere. Draw a circle about the size of an orange. Pick ONE light source (for example, upper left) and shade the circle so it reads as a solid ball. Show all four zones and label each one:

  • the highlight (brightest, near the light),
  • the midtone (the gradual middle gray),
  • the shadow (the dark side facing away from the light),
  • the cast shadow (the dark shape the ball throws onto the ground, opposite the light).

Try to blend smoothly from light to dark so no hard edge jumps out at you.

Submit: Photograph your sheet in good light (no shadow across the paper). Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive art portfolio folder: 2DArt_U04_Sketch_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort, auto/completion-scored):

  • Both parts present on the sheet
  • Value scale shows 5 distinct steps
  • Sphere uses one consistent light source
  • All four value zones are labeled
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: Value Landscape
assignments.html:
You have read a master's landscape. Now build your own, using nothing but light and dark. Draw a Value Landscape in black, white, and gray only. No color. The whole challenge is to make distance and form appear through value alone, the way Leonardo did with pen and ink.

Materials (home-accessible): drawing paper plus graphite pencils (a soft pencil helps you reach true darks), or a digital drawing app set to grayscale. Charcoal is welcome if you have it. Keep your full range available, from the white of the paper to your darkest dark.

Value focus: build clear atmospheric perspective and use one consistent light source throughout.

Steps:

  1. Choose a landscape: real, remembered, or invented. Plan three depth layers (background, middle ground, foreground).
  2. Make the sky lightest near the horizon so the air feels open.
  3. Draw background trees or hills the lightest values, soft and simple, so they read as far away.
  4. Give the middle ground a medium value with a little more detail.
  5. Make the foreground the darkest, with the most detail and overlap so it sits closest to the viewer.
  6. Keep one light source consistent across the whole scene, so shadows all fall the same way.
  7. Blend your value transitions smoothly where you want a soft, sfumato-like edge.
  8. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • The scene uses only black, white, and gray
  • A clear value range runs from the white of the paper to a true dark
  • Atmospheric perspective is visible: lightest in back, darkest in front
  • One light source is consistent throughout
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible
  • The work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • What is your landscape, and where is the light coming from?
  • Name where you placed your lightest and your darkest values, and why.
  • What are you proud of, or what would you change?

Submit: Photograph or export your finished landscape as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: 2DArt_U04_ValueLandscape_LastName.

assignments.title: Week 2 Studio Project: Personal Identity Collage + Artist Statement
assignments.html:
You have seen how Matisse built a whole work from just a few cut shapes and the empty space around them, drawing on a personal memory to do it. Now do the same to say something true about who you are. Create a Personal Identity Collage: a cut-paper collage that uses organic and geometric shapes, with deliberate positive shape and negative space, to express something about you. Your interests, your personality, where you are from, what matters to you.

Materials (home-accessible): scissors, glue or tape, a sheet of paper or cardstock for the background, and any colored paper you can gather (construction paper, magazine pages, junk mail, painted scrap, wrapping paper). A digital collage app that lets you cut and arrange shapes is an equally accepted option.

Shape focus: use both organic and geometric shapes, and treat the negative space as part of the design, not leftover background.

Steps:

  1. Brainstorm three to five things that say something about you. Do not write words. Think about what shape each idea could become.
  2. Cut your shapes freehand from colored paper, the way Matisse did. Make some organic, some geometric. Cut bold, simple shapes that would still read as silhouettes.
  3. Arrange the shapes on your background before gluing. Move them around. Pay attention to the negative space between them and let it guide the eye.
  4. When the arrangement feels balanced and expressive, glue everything down.
  5. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • Both organic and geometric shapes are used on purpose
  • Positive shapes and negative space are clearly and deliberately balanced
  • The shapes express something real about you
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible in the cutting and gluing
  • The work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • What does your collage say about you?
  • Name one organic and one geometric shape you used, and what each represents.
  • How did you use negative space on purpose?

Submit: Photograph or export your finished collage as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: 2DArt_U06_IdentityCollage_LastName.

assignments.title: Week 1 Sketch: Texture Sampler
assignments.html:
This sketch is your practice rung, not a finished artwork. You are stocking your toolbox of marks so they are ready when you draw your animal next week. Focus on control and variety, not perfection (~30 minutes total).

Set up your grid. On one sheet, draw a grid of 9 boxes, each about 1.5 inches square (3 rows of 3). You only need a pencil or pen.

Fill each box with a different mark-made texture. Use a separate technique in every box. Pick from these and invent a few of your own:

  • hatching (parallel lines)
  • cross-hatching (crossed layers of lines)
  • stippling (dots)
  • scribbling (loose looping lines)
  • short broken dashes
  • tiny circles or scales
  • wavy parallel lines
  • a pattern that copies a real surface (bark, fur, scales, feathers, stone)

Push the value range. In at least two boxes, start light on one edge and pack the marks tighter toward the other edge so the texture also shifts from light to dark.

Submit: Photograph your sheet in good light (no shadow across the paper). Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive art portfolio folder: 2DArt_U07_Sketch_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort, completion-scored):

  • All 9 boxes are filled
  • Each box uses a clearly different texture
  • At least two boxes show a light-to-dark value shift
  • Genuine effort and control are visible

assignments.title: Week 2 Studio Project: Texture Animal Drawing
assignments.html:
You have studied how Van Gogh built texture with thick paint, and you have built a toolbox of marks. Now put them to work. Draw a single animal and divide it into sections, filling each section with a different mark-made texture.

Materials (home-accessible): drawing paper and a pencil or pen. A black fine-tip marker works well for crisp marks. A digital drawing app with a stylus is an equally accepted option. This is a mark-making project, so color is optional.

Element focus: texture, with deliberate use of hatching, cross-hatching, stippling, and scribbling. Let your marks also control value so some sections read darker than others.

Steps (work through these in order; each builds on the last):

  1. Choose your animal. Pick an animal with an interesting silhouette: a fish, owl, elephant, peacock, fox, beetle, or anything you like.
  2. Sketch it big. Lightly draw the animal so it fills most of the page. Keep the outline simple for now. You are not adding any texture yet.
  3. Plan your sections. Lightly divide the animal into at least six sections that follow its natural shapes (the wing, the belly, the legs, the face, the tail). Draw these as light pencil lines you can still see through.
  4. Choose a texture for each section, before you start marking. Decide which mark-making technique goes in each section. No two neighboring sections should use the same mark.
  5. Match marks to real surfaces where it helps. Where it makes sense, let your mark suggest the real thing: scribbles for fur, small repeated curves for scales, stippling for a rough or speckled patch.
  6. Ink or draw the first half of your sections. Work section by section rather than the whole animal at once, so each texture stays controlled and clearly separate from its neighbor.
  7. Complete the remaining sections. Finish filling in every section, checking as you go that neighboring textures still read as clearly different from one another.
  8. Control your value across the whole drawing. Go back over the piece and pack your marks tighter in shadow areas, spreading them out in the light, so the animal reads as solid, not flat. Confirm the animal fills the page.
  9. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • At least six sections, each a clearly different mark-made texture
  • The marks are controlled and deliberate, not rushed
  • Value shifts (dense vs. open marks) give the animal solidity
  • The animal fills the page
  • The work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • What animal did you draw, and which textures did you use where?
  • Name one section where your marks worked exactly the way you wanted.
  • What would you change or push further next time?

Submit: Photograph or export your finished drawing as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: 2DArt_U07_TextureAnimal_LastName.

assignments.title: Week 1 Sketch: Shade the Four Solids
assignments.html:
This sketch is your practice rung, not a finished artwork. Sculptors and painters both start by training the eye to see solids and the way light falls on them. Focus on effort and observation, not perfection. Do all four on one sheet of paper (about 30 minutes total).

The task. Draw four shapes in a row: a circle, a square, a triangle, and a tall rectangle. Then turn each one into a form by shading it.

  1. Decide on ONE light source and mark it with a small arrow at the top of your page (for example, light coming from the upper left). Keep that same light for all four.
  2. Turn the circle into a sphere, the square into a cube, the triangle into a cone, and the rectangle into a cylinder.
  3. On the curved solids (sphere, cone, cylinder), shade with a smooth gradient from light to dark. On the cube, let the values jump from plane to plane.
  4. On at least one solid, label the highlight (brightest spot) and the shadow (darkest area). Add a cast shadow on the ground under each form.

Submit: Photograph your sheet in good, even light (no shadow across the paper). Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive art portfolio folder: 2DArt_U08_Sketch_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort, completion-scored):

  • All four solids attempted on one sheet
  • One consistent light source is marked
  • Curved solids show a gradient; the cube shows distinct planes
  • Highlight and shadow are labeled on at least one solid
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: Week 2 Studio Project: Water Droplet Drawing + Artist Statement
assignments.html:
You have shaded the four solids and watched value turn a flat circle into a sphere. Now use that skill on one of the most satisfying form studies in drawing: a water droplet that looks so round and wet it could roll off the page.

A droplet is a clear dome of water sitting on a surface. It is really a sphere problem with two twists: it is see-through, so it carries a tiny bright highlight and a glow of reflected light, and it bends what is behind it.

Materials (home-accessible): drawing paper, a pencil and eraser (a softer pencil helps with the darks), and an optional blending tool such as a tissue or a cotton swab. A digital drawing app with layers and a soft brush is an equally accepted option.

What to draw: one large water droplet, or a small group of two to three droplets, on a simple surface (a leaf, a tabletop, a window). Bigger is easier than tiny.

Steps:

  1. Pick ONE light source and stick with it. Lightly outline the droplet's rounded shape.
  2. Find the highlight: the small, brightest spot where the light hits the curved top. Leave the paper white there, or lift it out with your eraser.
  3. Build the value gradient across the droplet so it swells outward, darker where it curves away from the light.
  4. Add the core shadow inside the droplet and a cast shadow on the surface beneath it, usually on the side away from the light.
  5. Add the reflected light: a faint glow along the droplet's shadow edge, where light bounces back up from the surface. This is what makes water look wet and clear rather than solid.
  6. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • The droplet reads clearly as a 3-D form, not a flat outline
  • One consistent light source governs the whole drawing

assignments.title: Week 1 Sketch: Notan Thumbnail Studies
assignments.html:
This sketch is your practice rung, not a finished artwork. Notan designers always thumbnail first, because a small two-value sketch tells you instantly whether a composition is balanced. Focus on the light-and-dark relationship, not on detail (about 30 minutes total).

The task. On one sheet of paper, draw 2 to 3 small squares, each about 2 inches wide. Inside each square, design a different composition using only two values: leave the white of the paper as your light, and fill the dark areas solidly with pencil, marker, or black paint. No gray, no shading, no color.

Try a different balance of positive and negative space in each one:

  • one square mostly light with a few dark shapes,
  • one square mostly dark with a few light shapes,
  • one square as close to half-and-half as you can manage.

Under each square, write one word for what it makes you think of, then squint at it to test whether the design still reads when blurry.

Submit: Photograph your sheet in good light (no shadow across the paper). Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive art portfolio folder: 2DArt_U09_Sketch_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort, completion-scored):

  • 2 to 3 thumbnail squares present
  • Each uses two values only (clear light and clear dark)
  • Each shows a different positive/negative balance
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: Week 1 VR Session: Japanese Art Gallery Critique
assignments.html:
Before you enter: Have your vocabulary list (positive space, negative space, figure-ground, notan) and the four DAIJ steps (Describe, Analyze, Interpret, Judge) ready. Then choose the woodblock print you will critique this week.

Pick ONE real Japanese woodblock print from the list below, or bring a different print or Japanese design of your own choosing if you already have one in mind (get it approved by your teacher first):

  • Katsushika Hokusai, Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave), from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, ca. 1830 to 32. The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
  • Katsushika Hokusai, South Wind, Clear Sky ("Red Fuji"), from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, ca. 1830 to 32. The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
  • Utagawa Hiroshige, Sudden Shower over Shin-Ohashi Bridge and Atake, from One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, 1857. The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

Look up your chosen print and find a clear image of it. Bring that image into your own VR space yourself, using whatever image or content import tool your VR app provides. You may choose any gallery Location you like.

Part 1 — Look (about 10 min). Place your chosen print where you can move close to study it and step back to see it whole. Using your VR drawing or note tool, place short notes beside it answering:

  1. Describe: What is literally shown?
  2. Analyze: Where is the positive space, and where is the negative space? Which one is larger?
  3. Interpret: What feeling does the empty space create?
  4. Judge: Does the balance of full and empty work? Why?

Part 2 — Make (about 10 min). Use the VR drawing tool to build a simple two-value composition in the air: block in a few dark shapes against the open light, and arrange them so the empty areas feel deliberate, not leftover. This is a notan study in space.

Part 3 — Respond (about 5 min). Answer aloud (record a short voice note) or in writing: "If you removed the empty space from the print you studied, what would the picture lose?" If you are in a live session, share with a classmate and respond to one other answer.

Submit: Take a screenshot inside VR showing your chosen print, your critique notes, or your two-value composition, and upload it. (No screenshot tool? Write 2 to 3 sentences describing what you did, including which print you chose.) Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder.

Grading: Completion. Evidence that a real print was chosen and brought into VR, and that all three parts were attempted.

assignments.title: Week 2 Studio Project: Notan Design + Artist Statement
assignments.html:
You have seen how Hokusai made empty space carry a whole ocean. Now build your own balance of light and dark using the classic notan cut-and-flip method. The trick of this project: the black shapes you cut out and the white spaces they leave behind are equal partners. Nothing is wasted.

Materials (home-accessible): one square of black paper (about 6 inches), one square of white paper (slightly larger), scissors, and a glue stick. No black paper? Color a white square solid black, or work in a digital drawing app using a black layer and a white background.

The cut-and-flip method:

  1. Start with your black square centered on your white square, but do not glue it yet.
  2. Cut a shape inward from one edge of the black square. Do not cut shapes out of the middle and throw them away. Cut from an edge so the piece stays attached or can be flipped outward.
  3. Flip each cut piece straight out across the edge it came from, like opening a door, and set it on the white paper next to the gap it left.
  4. Repeat on the other edges. Each black shape that flips out leaves an equal white shape behind. That mirrored balance is the heart of notan.
  5. Step back and squint. The black masses and the white masses should feel balanced, with negative space that reads as its own shape, not as leftover.
  6. When the balance works, glue everything down.
  7. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

Element focus: space, worked as positive (the black shapes) and negative (the white shapes), with deliberate figure-ground balance.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • The design uses two values only, clean black and clean white
  • Shapes are flipped, so the positive and negative areas mirror and balance
  • The negative space reads as its own shape, not as empty leftover
  • The composition still reads when you squint (a strong notan)
  • The work is neat, fully glued, complete, and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • What do your shapes suggest, and what mood does the balance create?
  • Point to one place where the negative space became its own shape.
  • What are you proud of, or what would you change?

Submit: Photograph or scan your finished notan as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: 2DArt_U09_Notan_LastName.
